episode_summary: June 2019 episode of The Bitcoin Podcast with no interview. The hosts discuss the HODL+ rebalancing strategy, Facebook's Libra announcement and whitepaper, whether Libra helps or hurts crypto adoption, virtue signaling and scams aimed at influencers, and how much of crypto trading volume is real.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host credited Facebook's Libra code with reasonable consensus choices, using classical BFT rather than Nakamoto consensus.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: They chose reasonable choices in the consensus mechanism, given its classical BFT and nothing like Nakamoto consensus or anything new.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said Libra was more decentralized than anything that had existed in the traditional financial world, though not pure crypto.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: at least well done, and it's more decentralized than anything that's ever existed from the traditional world.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host argued Libra was just a distributed ledger, with nothing new in principle because banks already move value quickly.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Well, that's redundant because T in DLT is technology. But, like, it's a distributed ledger. That's it.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said Libra was not open, permissionless consensus, which the host called the foundation of blockchain.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: it's just not it's not open and permissionless consensus that's kind of the foundation

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said Libra's whitepaper is not block-based and gives instant finality like Hyperledger, so it does not need blocks.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: It's basically like the Hyperledger system where it's instant finality because they don't need blocks to actually do a blockchain.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said Libra was most similar to Ripple in its design.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: It's the main thing it's probably closest to is Ripple.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said that if Libra drove mass adoption, crypto fans would be unhappy about it, though he did not expect it to last.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: if something you don't like spurs mass adoption you guys aren't going to be very happy about it

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host predicted that better open, permissionless governance systems would eventually bring privatized systems like Libra to their knees.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: I think eventually something's going to happen. It's going to bring that to its knees.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host argued that a centralized system like Libra could not handle global IoT microtransaction volume, and that decentralization scales better.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: you're not going to successfully accomplish that with this centralized system i don't believe you will i believe that decentralization is the way to go with that just because it scales better eventually

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host doubted Libra would be a long-term supportable system in its drafted form.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: i have real doubts that like this will actually be a long-term supportable thing in his current the way it's currently drafted

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said Facebook had been trying to become a bank for about six years through money services licenses.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: The thing is that Facebook has been trying to be a bank for like six years now.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host objected that no one voted for Facebook to hold sovereign decision-making power over money on a global scale.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Just from an ethical standpoint, it seems like I didn't vote them into having sovereign decision-making power over money on a global scale.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host described Libra's planned validators as a cartel of $10 million members that Facebook would approve.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: There's a whole bunch of people working together in this cartel of $10 million validators who Facebook can approve or disapprove of

cards.claim: In June 2019 a guest called Libra potentially a Trojan horse that could draw people toward Bitcoin and other cryptocurrency.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I really feel like Libra is potentially potentially a Trojan horse for Bitcoin and other cryptocurrency

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said the Libra news was a catalyst for the Bitcoin price action that week, drawing sidelined investors back in.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: it was a catalyst for a lot of the price action we've seen around Bitcoin as well

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said the Winklevoss twins probably held a little more than one percent of all bitcoin.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: pretty sure they're a little bit higher than one percent now

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host predicted that if bitcoin reached $10,000 the Winklevoss twins would be worth one to three billion dollars.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: goes up to ten thousand then they're probably looking at one to three billion dollars in net worth

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host warned that scammers would flood Facebook Messenger, and that bots and social engineers would target grandparents' bank access.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Scam city. Scam city is coming. But imagine when your grandma and your great aunt are on Facebook with instant access to their banking funds.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host argued Facebook's reversible transactions and fund tracing could let it detect and stop scammers.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: going directly through the scammers can actually give them a good detection and uh like ability to actually stop this kind of behavior.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said his big fear was a global digital-money event that would produce an authoritarian reaction.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: My big fear is it happens on a global scale and the reaction to that will be very authoritarian

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host predicted that Libra would make for a weird future if it launched by 2020.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: it's going to be a weird future once this comes out, if they actually get it out by 2020.

cards.claim: In June 2019 the hosts defined virtue signaling as showing you have virtue by expressing disgust.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: it's a person who shows you they have virtue by expressing disgust

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host argued that crypto unites self-interest with collective benefit, so it is the answer to trickle-down economics.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: for the first time in history humans have come up with a system that manages to unite self-interest with a collective benefit so you have capitalism united with socialism

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said he would not take paid promotions because his credibility as an educator and security engineer depends on not being for sale.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: I personally won't do it because that's part of my reputation. I don't say things that I don't believe ever.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said that paying an influencer to push a bad wallet ruins their reputation, unlike a sponsor with no bearing on the talk.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: But if someone pays you $25,000 to say, oh, go buy this wallet. It's the best, most secure wallet out there, and that's not necessarily true, then you've ruined a lot of your reputation

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said the Ethereum community seemed grandstandy, with many people tweeting about imposter syndrome.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: I think a lot of the Ethereum community, this is my personal on the outside looking in is a lot of I don't know, seems a little grandstandy.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said much of crypto trading volume was people betting on price moves without understanding the underlying asset.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: A good portion of the volume, if not the majority of the volume, of cryptocurrencies is people moving it back and forth, betting on what the price is going to do

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host guessed about 75 percent of crypto trading volume came from people other than genuine individual investors, with no research behind it.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: 75%. Oh, wow. That's my very naive rough guess with no real research behind it.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said that on breached exchanges wash trading was closer to 95 percent, though the data was flawed.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: The exchanges that have been breached, the ones that their data has actually been dumped, it's closer to like 95% because there's so much shenanigans going on.

cards.claim: In June 2019 the hosts described QuadrigaCX as a scam from day zero, citing auditor reports that it traded with customer money.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: It turns out that was a scam from day zero.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host predicted derivatives would bring fresh attention to crypto, the same way Libra had, as people turned from fiat to crypto.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Like the second a back drops, everybody's going to bow face and look away from Fiat

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host explained HODL+ as taking some fiat out of bitcoin at a high price, then rebalancing back to the target percentages.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: And whenever those percentages gets out of whack, you basically rebalance back to what your original starting percentages was.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said HODL was a misspelling of hold that the community adopted long ago.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Somebody misspelled hold a long time ago and we ran with it.

cards.claim: In June 2019 a host said his average bitcoin entry price was under $1,000.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: So my average entry price is sub $1,000.

title: The Bitcoin Podcast #263
